primary_topics: Monthly luncheon fellowship address to the Philippine Bar Association (PBA), March 26, 2014 -- calling on lawyers to help safeguard liberty, conquer poverty, and nurture prosperity

The rapidly changing world: communications (land lines to Viber/Skype/social media), medicine (quacks to stem cells and eternity), business (proprietorships to multinationals), politics (monarchy to liberal democracy) -- all demanding a new legal response

The economic rights argument: the same vigor shown by the judiciary in protecting political/civil rights should be applied to economic rights -- the WTO Tanada v. Angara case as CJP's definitive articulation of the deferential interpretation doctrine on economic matters

Globalizing the legal profession: Rule 138 of the Rules of Court limiting bar admission to Filipino citizens and residents is outdated given ASEAN integration; foreign lawyers should be allowed to practice on limited, reciprocal terms; the PBA should spearhead updating Rule 138
sub_topics: PBA Award of Honor (April 26, 2007): cited as 'a principled and visionary leader by example; a prolific writer of the Supreme Court, bar none; a renaissance man; a nobly-souled and gifted jurist; over 250 awards; an exemplary family man'

Communications revolution: from land lines to colored TV, telex, fax, cell phones, SMS, PCs, Internet, email; then Viber/Magic Jack, Skype, social media; now sniping, CCTVs, YouTube, GPS, drones, robots; 'soon, newspapers, land lines, movie houses, the post office and even our constitutionally-protected privacy will disappear'

Medicine revolution: physicians healing diseases; then preventing illnesses (isolation/vaccinations); then well-being and beauty; now biotechnologies and stem cell research promoting longevity and even eternity ('regenerate worn or destroyed human tissues and organs')

Business evolution: single proprietorships, partnerships, giant corporations, conglomerates, multinationals; 'at times, conglomerates and multinationals become more powerful than governments' -- Lehman Brothers collapse cited

Constitutional history: Americans built nation during political independence struggle; Patrick Henry's 'Give me liberty or give me death'; Philippine Constitutions (Malolos to 1987) all drafted during political freedom struggles; even the SC's Miranda rights written into the text of the 1987 Constitution (not in the US Constitution)

Disini v. Sec. of Justice (Feb. 18, 2014): SC struck down several Cybercrimes Prevention Law provisions; Abad ponencia + Sereno, Carpio, Brion, Leonen opinions cited as 'sumptuous feasts for constitutional law scholars'
Manila Hotel/Manila Prince v. GSIS (Feb. 3, 1997): SC voided a public auction won by a foreign company; preference for losing Filipino bidder; CJP was a dissenter
Economic nationalism in 1987 and WTO in 1995: 'Filipino First'; government-owned corporations (NPC lost almost a trillion pesos); then WTO liberated the world from protectionism

Tanada v. Angara (May 2, 1997): CJP's ponencia upholding WTO; 'while the Constitution mandates a bias in favor of Filipino goods... it allows an exchange on the basis of equality and reciprocity'; strict scrutiny for civil liberties; deferential interpretation for economic matters

Gamboa v. Teves (June 28, 2011 per Carpio): 40% foreign ownership in public utilities limited to voting shares; CJP urges prospective application for investors who relied on DOJ/SEC interpretation in good faith

Initiatives for Dialogue v. PSALM (Oct. 9, 2012 per Villarama): river water = national resource for Filipinos; but once 'appropriated by a qualified local company and collected in a dam' = private; Korean firm may use it for electricity generation
Textualists vs. living Constitution (same Scalia-Kennedy anecdote as SB075)

Rule 138 and foreign lawyers: Philippine conglomerates now operate abroad (SM, BDO, Metrobank, Jollibee, Cebu Pacific, ICTSI etc.); they need Filipino lawyers abroad; 'foreign lawyers should be allowed to practice here, but not about Philippine law... but about foreign law where their foreign clients originate or operate in, provided there is reciprocity'

Dean Andres Bautista's Hopewell Holdings example: $1.2 billion power plant in Sual, Pangasinan; Clifford Chance 'fly-in, fly-out' lawyers from New York and Hong Kong; question: are they already practicing Philippine law under Cayetano v. Monsod's expansive definition?
ASEAN integration 2015: single market for goods, investments, capital, skilled labor and services; 10 million OFWs remitting $26 billion; 1 million BPO workers remitting $16 billion

The ethics section: shyster-lawyers who deliberately delay cases (witnesses forget, judges retire, victims give up); corrupt prosecutors (defective informations, omitting vital evidence, fraudulent document loss, frequent absences; filing baseless charges -- 'not only unethical. It is brazenly criminal.')

Three closing calls: rededication to competent and ethical practice; fresh look at globalizing political and economic rights; legal profession to help safeguard liberty AND conquer poverty AND nurture prosperity

stances.claim: Rule 138's restriction on bar admission to Filipino citizens and Philippine residents is outdated and should be updated by the PBA to allow foreign lawyers to practice on a limited, reciprocal basis -- practicing only foreign law (not Philippine law) as the equivalent of English 'solicitors' not 'barristers,' provided their home countries give Filipino lawyers the same privilege. This is the actionable reform CJP calls on the PBA to spearhead.
stances.rhetorical_move: ASEAN-integration-as-urgency: the 2015 single market deadline as the reason Rule 138 must be updated now, with Dean Bautista's Hopewell example as the concrete problem the rule fails to solve
stances.confidence: asserted as a specific legislative/rule reform proposal with four conditions

stances.claim: Filing baseless criminal charges -- whether for money or malice -- is 'not only unethical. It is brazenly criminal.' This is CJP's strongest condemnation of a specific legal profession maleficence, going beyond ethical violations to characterize the conduct as a crime against the accused.
stances.rhetorical_move: criminal-not-just-unethical characterization: escalating the ethical standard to a legal duty with criminal consequences
stances.confidence: asserted as a categorical moral-legal judgment

stances.claim: The same vigor shown by courts in protecting political rights should be applied to economic rights -- 'how I wish' is CJP's acknowledging the gap. Tanada v. Angara established the deferential interpretation doctrine on economic matters, but the judiciary and the legal profession still default to political rights as the primary register.
stances.rhetorical_move: parallel-vigor argument: the political-rights enforcement standard as the benchmark the legal profession should meet on economic rights
stances.confidence: asserted as an aspirational standard with acknowledged gap

notable_anecdotes: The technology-privacy prediction: 'soon, newspapers, land lines, movie houses, the post office and even our constitutionally-protected privacy will disappear' -- CJP's most prescient forecast in the corpus, delivered in 2014.

Dean Bautista's Hopewell-Clifford Chance example (February 7, 2014): Hopewell Holdings (HK) building a $1.2 billion power plant in Sual, Pangasinan; financed by IFC, Japan Ex-Im Bank and others; loan documents governed by New York laws; Clifford Chance lawyers 'fly in and fly out' from New York and Hong Kong to negotiate. Question under Cayetano v. Monsod: are they already practicing Philippine law?

OFW scale: 10 million OFWs remitting $26 billion; 1 million BPO workers remitting $16 billion -- the Philippines' people as its primary export, necessitating Filipino lawyers who can follow them abroad.

Shysters who deliberately delay: 'they defend the indefensible by deliberately delaying cases in the hope that the witnesses against their clients may forget the facts, or get tired, or die; or that presiding judges may retire, or get promoted thereby passing the cases to new magistrates who had no opportunity to observe the witnesses on the stand' -- a detailed taxonomy of delay-as-defense.

The Scalia-Kennedy dialogue (same as SB075 but with additional detail: Scalia explicitly said 'I do not believe in international law. When I joined the US Supreme Court, I swore to defend the US Constitution and nothing else.')

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered March 26, 2014 at the Philippine Bar Association's monthly luncheon fellowship at the Tower Club, Makati -- CJP accepting due to gratitude for the PBA's 2007 Award of Honor -- this address surveys four rapidly changing domains (communications: from land lines to Viber, Skype and social media, ending in the prediction that 'newspapers, land lines, movie houses, the post office and even our constitutionally-protected privacy will disappear'; medicine: from healing to preventing to longevity to 'eternity' via stem cells; business: proprietorships to multinationals more powerful than governments; politics: monarchy to liberal democracy born from Patrick Henry's 'Give me liberty or give me death'). He notes the jurisprudential tension: the SC showed 'vigor and vitality in promoting political rights' in Disini v. Sec. of Justice (Cybercrimes, Feb 2014); he wishes the same would be shown for economic rights. His Tanada v. Angara (May 1997) ponencia is presented as the definitive answer: strict scrutiny for civil liberties; deferential interpretation on economic matters; private enterprise as the engine; the economic pie must be enlarged, not just divided. He comments on Manila Prince v. GSIS (Manila Hotel; CJP dissented), Gamboa v. Teves (40% foreign ownership in utilities limited to voting shares -- urges prospective application), and Initiatives for Dialogue v. PSALM (river water nationalized but private once dammed). The textualist-vs-living-Constitution debate is illustrated with the Scalia-Kennedy anecdote. The substantive reform proposal: Rule 138's restriction on bar admission to Filipinos and Philippine residents is outdated given ASEAN 2015 integration, 10 million OFWs ($26 billion) and 1 million BPO workers ($16 billion); Dean Bautista's Hopewell-Clifford Chance example (Hong Kong developer, New York-law loans, fly-in-fly-out lawyers) shows the rule's inadequacy under Cayetano v. Monsod's expansive practice-of-law definition. CJP proposes four conditions for allowing limited foreign practice. He closes with an ethics charge -- shysters who deliberately delay cases and prosecutors who file baseless charges ('not only unethical, it is brazenly criminal') -- and three calls: rededication to competent and ethical practice; fresh look at globalizing political and economic rights; and for the legal profession to help safeguard liberty AND conquer poverty AND nurture prosperity.
